objects.name: CTFT Project
objects.description: Capture-The-Flag Techniques - an ontology of CTF solving behaviour. Relates to MITRE ATT&CK, CAPEC and CWE as per-entry anchors; not a parallel ATT&CK. Generalized from FOM.

objects.name: Forensics
objects.description: Challenges where the flag survives in an artifact but not in plain sight: tampered file signatures, slack and unallocated space, falsified timestamps, alternate data streams, memory images, packet captures and unusual encodings. Recovery is structural — read what the container actually is, not what it claims to be. (HTB: Forensics)

objects.name: CTFTTE-FOR-001 - Magic-byte / file-signature tampering

objects.name: CTFTCTE-FOR-001 - Recover the legitimate file signature
objects.description: Compare bytes against a signature table, identify the true type from structure/footers, and patch the header with a hex editor or python.
Counter-technique recovers/defeats the paired design technique. `mitigates` is kept for STIX-consumer compatibility; the CTFT semantics are carried by x_ctft_relation.

objects.name: CTFTCTE-FOR-007 - Recover legitimate signature of a file
objects.description: Recover legitimate signature of a file, often called magic headers. Magic headers, also known as file signatures, are specific byte sequences located at the beginning of a file that help identify the file type. These headers are used by operating systems and applications to determine how to process or open a file.
Counter-technique recovers/defeats the paired design technique. `mitigates` is kept for STIX-consumer compatibility; the CTFT semantics are carried by x_ctft_relation.

objects.name: CTFTTE-FOR-008 - OpenEXR header-signature tampering
objects.description: Modify magic headers via python script import zlib import struct def fixpngfile(filepath, outputpath): with open(filepath, 'rb') as file: data = file.read() # Replace modified header modifiedheader = b'\x89RNG' correctheader = b'\x89PNG' if data.startswith(modifiedheader): data = correctheader + data[len(modifiedheader):] else: print("Modified header not found.") return # Function to check and fix CRCs of PNG chunks def fixcrc(data): pos = 8 # Skip the first 8 bytes (header) fixeddata = data[:pos] while pos < len(data): chunklength = struct.unpack('>I', data[pos:pos+4])[0] chunktype = data[pos+4:pos+8] chunkdata = data[pos+8:pos+8+chunklength] chunkcrc = struct.unpack('>I', data[pos+8+chunklength:pos+12+chunklength])[0] # Calculate the correct CRC calculatedcrc = zlib.crc32(chunktype) calculatedcrc = zlib.crc32(chunkdata, calculatedcrc) calculatedcrc = calculatedcrc & 0xffffffff if chunkcrc != calculatedcrc: print(f"Fixing CRC for chunk: {chunktype.decode('ascii')}") fixeddata += struct.pack('>I', chunklength) + chunktype + chunkdata + struct.pack('>I', calculatedcrc) else: fixeddata += data[pos:pos+12+chunklength] pos += 12 + chunklength return fixeddata # Fix CRCs data = fixcrc(data) # Save the fixed file with open(outputpath, 'wb') as outputfile: outputfile.write(data) print(f"File saved as {outputpath}") # Use the function with your file fixpngfile('magicrepairman.png', '2fixedmagicrepairman.png')

objects.name: CTFTCTE-FOR-008 - Recover legitimate header signature of an OpenEXR image file

Counter-technique recovers/defeats the paired design technique. `mitigates` is kept for STIX-consumer compatibility; the CTFT semantics are carried by x_ctft_relation.

objects.name: CTFTCTE-FOR-009 - Repair a corrupted image magic signature
objects.description: Read the first bytes with a hex editor and compare them against the signature table for the extension claimed by the file name. When the magic is corrupted rather than merely wrong, the rest of the container is usually intact: rewrite the expected signature in place and re-open the file. For PNG also check the IHDR chunk and the trailing IEND; for JPEG the SOI/EOI markers. If several candidate types fit, carve the file and let the structural parser decide.

objects.name: CTFTTE-FOR-027 - Use JAB colour 2D codes to hide data
objects.description: The payload is encoded as a JAB Code (Just Another Barcode): a colour 2D matrix symbology whose modules are coloured squares laid out on square or rectangular grids. Because the data lives in the colour channel rather than in black-and-white modules, ordinary QR readers ignore the symbol entirely, and a greyscale conversion or an aggressive JPEG recompression destroys the payload without any visible sign of damage.

objects.name: CTFTCTE-FOR-027 - Retrieve information from JAB colour codes
objects.description: JAB Code (Just Another Barcode) is a colour 2D matrix symbology made of colour squares arranged in either square or rectangular grids. Decode with the reference jabcode reader rather than a QR library. Work from the highest-fidelity copy available: the colour palette carries data, so any greyscale conversion, palette reduction or lossy recompression is destructive.
Counter-technique recovers/defeats the paired design technique. `mitigates` is kept for STIX-consumer compatibility; the CTFT semantics are carried by x_ctft_relation.

objects.name: CTFTTE-FOR-028 - Windows event-log evidence concealment
objects.description: The answer lives in the Windows event logs and nowhere else: the author supplies a full Logs/ tree of .evtx channels and hides the decisive record among tens of thousands of routine ones. Concealment is by volume and by channel choice — the interesting event sits in an operational or application channel rather than Security, its provider is unremarkable, and neighbouring records are legitimate. Variants clear a channel, disable a provider, or roll the log so the record survives only in a companion channel.

objects.name: CTFTCTE-FOR-028 - Reconstruct the timeline from Windows event logs
objects.description: Do not read channels one by one. Normalise the whole Logs/ tree into a single time-ordered table (EvtxECmd to CSV, or python-evtx to JSON), then pivot: filter on the window the challenge frames, then on providers that should be quiet. Records that matter are usually the ones whose channel does not match their content — a scripting engine event in an application channel, a service install outside a maintenance window. Gaps matter as much as records: a channel that stops and resumes marks a clearing.
Counter-technique recovers/defeats the paired design technique. `mitigates` is kept for STIX-consumer compatibility; the CTFT semantics are carried by x_ctft_relation.

objects.name: CTFTTE-FOR-029 - Registry-hive persistence artifact concealment
objects.description: The flag or the decisive indicator is a persistence entry inside a Windows registry hive, and the hive is delivered inside a forensic container (AD1, E01, raw) rather than as a loose file. The author counts on two barriers: the container format, which ordinary tools will not open, and the value itself, whose payload is encoded — typically a Run key holding a base64 PowerShell stager. The surrounding hive is legitimate, so nothing looks out of place until the value is decoded.

objects.name: CTFTCTE-FOR-029 - Extract and analyse registry hives from a forensic image
objects.description: Open the container first: AD1 is AccessData's logical image format and FTK Imager exports its tree directly; for E01 use ewfmount, for raw images mount read-only. Extract SOFTWARE, SYSTEM, NTUSER.DAT and their transaction logs, then parse offline with Registry Explorer or python-registry. Go straight to the autostart surface — Run, RunOnce, Services, scheduled task caches — and decode every value that is not plain text. A base64 blob in a Run value is the payload, not the answer: decode it and read what it does.
Counter-technique recovers/defeats the paired design technique. `mitigates` is kept for STIX-consumer compatibility; the CTFT semantics are carried by x_ctft_relation.

objects.name: CTFTTE-FOR-030 - Read-triggered payload mutation (guardian process)
objects.description: A background guardian process (e.g. flag-defender) watches the flag file and re-encrypts it on every access — XOR with the current time, content doubling in size with each read. The concealment is the act of reading itself: every observation changes the ciphertext, so CyberChef magic, hash comparison and format detection all fail, and naive triage burns instance re-provisionings. The defense punishes the standard forensic loop (open → inspect → decode) and only reveals itself through repeated identical reads producing different bytes.

objects.name: CTFTCTE-FOR-030 - Detect, stop and snapshot a read-triggered mutator
objects.description: 1. Read the file twice with no other access in between; diff the two reads. Growth or change on identical reads proves a mutator — do not waste re-provisionings on decoding. 2. Find the guardian: process inventory (ps auxww), open handles (/proc//fd pointing at the file or its directory), and inotify/fanotify watchers (/proc//fdinfo). 3. Terminate the guardian (as root if needed) and immediately snapshot the file to a timestamped copy outside its watch path. 4. Treat the last-written state as the stable ciphertext and move to key recovery — the mutation often re-encrypts with a time-derived key, so the file's mtime is the next lead (see CTFTCTE-CRY-014).
Counter-technique recovers/defeats the paired design technique. `mitigates` is kept for STIX-consumer compatibility; the CTFT semantics are carried by x_ctft_relation.

objects.name: CTFTTE-FOR-031 - Office VBA macro string concealment
objects.description: The flag is placed inside a VBA macro embedded in a macro-enabled Office document (.docm, .xlsm, .doc). It is never present as plaintext: the macro rebuilds it at run time from obfuscated pieces — character-code arrays (Chr(72) & Chr(84) & ...), StrReverse, split-and-concatenate, base64 or XOR routines — so opening the document and reading the visible text yields nothing, and the string does not survive a plain strings pass over the ZIP container. The concealment leans on the analyst either trusting the rendered document or lacking Office to "run" the macro.

external_references.description: Command and Scripting Interpreter: Visual Basic

objects.name: CTFTCTE-FOR-031 - Extract and decode strings from Office VBA macros
objects.description: 1. Confirm the container: a .docm/.xlsm is a ZIP — unzip -l lists the parts and word/vbaProject.bin (or xl/vbaProject.bin) is the OLE stream holding the macros. 2. Dump the macro source without Office: olevba <file> extracts the VBA and highlights auto-exec entry points and string-building constructs; oledump.py dumps the raw stream bytes when olevba can't parse a mangled project. 3. Read the deobfuscation olevba already performed; for anything it leaves, reproduce the macro's own transform by hand — evaluate the Chr()/StrReverse/concat chain, or feed the base64/XOR argument to CyberChef. 4. If the macro only reconstructs the string at run time, port the VBA expression to Python (or run it in a sandboxed VBA host) and print the result instead of executing the rest.

external_references.description: Command and Scripting Interpreter: Visual Basic

objects.description: Counter-technique recovers/defeats the paired design technique. `mitigates` is kept for STIX-consumer compatibility; the CTFT semantics are carried by x_ctft_relation.

objects.name: CTFTTE-FOR-032 - Flag concealed in a haystack of near-identical files
objects.description: The flag (or the one meaningful file) is buried inside a very large archive of thousands of near-duplicate files — same size, same structure, mostly identical bytes — so that no single file stands out and manual inspection is infeasible. The concealment is scale plus sameness: grep for the flag format may miss an encoded fragment, and opening files one by one never terminates. The intended solve is a comparison that is efficient at scale — hash every file and keep the one whose content is unique, or diff against the common baseline — rather than reading each file.

objects.name: CTFTCTE-FOR-032 - Isolate the outlier file by scalable comparison
objects.description: 1. Do not read files individually. Reduce the haystack by content hash: find . -type f -exec sha256sum {} + | sort | uniq -c -w64 | sort -n — the line with count 1 (or the smallest counts) is the outlier whose bytes differ from the crowd. 2. If every file is unique but shares a common template, diff against a baseline instead: pick any file as reference and cmp/diff the rest, keeping only the one with a non-trivial delta. For fixed-size records, hash a byte range rather than the whole file. 3. When the difference is a single changed region, xxd the outlier and the baseline and compare the dumps to read the injected bytes directly. 4. This is the scalable equivalent of the original C++ comparison loop: hashing is O(n) over the corpus and never holds more than one file in memory, so it finishes on archives of tens of thousands of files.
Counter-technique recovers/defeats the paired design technique. `mitigates` is kept for STIX-consumer compatibility; the CTFT semantics are carried by x_ctft_relation.

objects.name: CTFTTE-FOR-033 - Flag fragments disseminated across filesystem artifacts
objects.description: No single file holds the flag. It is broken into pieces and scattered across many locations — individual characters embedded in shell-persistence files (.bashrc, cron entries, systemd units, /etc/), one letter per file in a tree, or fragments appended to otherwise innocuous logs. Each fragment on its own is meaningless, and the flag only appears once every piece is collected in the correct order. The concealment defeats a single-file search: the analyst has to recognise the dissemination pattern (which files, which position marks ordering) and reassemble, not just locate.

external_references.description: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution: Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder

objects.name: CTFTCTE-FOR-033 - Aggregate disseminated flag fragments across files
objects.description: 1. Sweep broadly first: grep -RnoaE 'HTB\{|flag\{|[A-Za-z0-9+/=]{3,}' . across the whole tree, and inventory the usual persistence carriers (.bashrc, .profile, crontab -l, /etc/cron., systemd units, /etc/passwd GECOS, log tails) where fragments are planted. 2. Identify the dissemination key — what ties the fragments together and in what order: a line number, a filename index, a timestamp, an array subscript in a script. One character per file usually means the ordering is the filename or path sort. 3. Reassemble deterministically rather than by eye: collect path:fragment pairs, sort by the ordering key, then concatenate the fragment column (sort -t: -k1 | cut -d: -f2 | tr -d '\n'). Decode the result if it is base64/hex. 4. Validate against the expected flag format; a wrong order or a missed carrier yields near-miss garbage, so re-check the ordering key before brute-forcing permutations.

external_references.description: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution: Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder

objects.name: CTFTTE-FOR-034 - Obfuscated client-side script in a web artifact
objects.description: A captured web artifact — a phishing page, a saved HTML file, an email attachment — carries a block of deliberately obfuscated JavaScript. The script is minified to one line, packed (eval(function(p,a,c,k,e,d)...)), and its strings are hex/base64/String.fromCharCode encoded, so the real behaviour (the exfiltration URL, the decoded flag, the dropped payload name) is not visible in the page source. Rendering the page runs the script but hides the mechanism; reading the source shows only noise. The analyst is meant to statically deobfuscate and follow the data flow to the hidden value rather than detonate the page.

objects.name: CTFTCTE-FOR-034 - Deobfuscate and trace client-side script to the payload
objects.description: 1. Isolate the script from the artifact (the <script> block, the .js file, the HTML attachment) and work on it statically — do not open the page in a live browser. 2. Restore structure first: run it through js-beautify to expand the one-liner, then de4js to unpack eval(p,a,c,k,e,d) and eval/Function wrappers into plain source. 3. Decode the string literals: String.fromCharCode, \xNN/\uNNNN, base64 and URL layers go through CyberChef. Follow the data flow to the sink — the fetch/XMLHttpRequest URL, the document.location redirect, or the variable printed/ concatenated into the DOM — which is where the flag or exfil target resolves. 4. If the script self-decodes at run time, neutralise the sink and evaluate it safely: replace eval/network calls with console.log and run under Node in a throwaway sandbox to print the decoded value instead of executing it.
Counter-technique recovers/defeats the paired design technique. `mitigates` is kept for STIX-consumer compatibility; the CTFT semantics are carried by x_ctft_relation.
